criteria.note: The TL;DR answers 'can a celiac travel in Korea and how' inside the first ~150 words — doable with prep, named dedicated-GF anchors, the allergy phrase, convenience-store baseline — and the next section is 'If You're Celiac, Start Here'.

Title is 'Celiac Travel in Korea: Field Guide' (33 chars) plus the appended ' | Gluten-Free Korea' = 53 chars, description is 146 chars, keyword present in both, and the only overlap is the keyword itself rather than repeated selling phrasing.

Headings carry the argument rather than label it ('What Korean Food Actually Looks Like, From a Gluten Angle', 'The One Phrase That Actually Works', 'Reading Korean Labels: Four Words That Matter'), so a heading-only skim yields the whole method.
Nine internal links, each placed where a reader would want the deeper page — phrases post at the phrase section, label guide at the barley caveat, snacks post at the chip list.

All five frontmatter Q/As are established in the body (tamari wheat caveat, 10%-wheat bakery anecdote, 237's unconfirmed status, BBQ grill contamination) and each answer reads standalone as a rich result.

Dense with observed specifics: a bakery owner's '90% rice flour, 10% wheat', a product renamed from 'gluten-free bread' to 'rice bread' a week after ordering, 237 found closed for remodelling, pink vs green Chamsal Seolbyeong packets, a dated call to the ssaltongdak franchise HQ.

Korean terms are given with hangul plus romanisation (간장 ganjang, 밀떡 mil-tteok, 뻥튀기 ppeongttwigi) and claims are pinned to checkable products (Goraesa eomuk, Poca Chip Original vs Onion, the 알레르기 유발물질 line vs 원재료명).
The two load-bearing regulatory/product claims link primary sources with a stated as-of date — the MFDS 식품등의 표시기준 (별표 2, in force August 2026) and Orion's own product page (re-verified August 2026).

The piece repeatedly states what its method cannot establish ('our standard is NCGS, and we can't audit a kitchen', a removed GFCO claim, 'we haven't personally verified it'), and carries no affiliate or commercial links needing disclosure.

findings.quote: Updated August 2026: added the MFDS labeling-standard and manufacturer citations, dated our franchise call
findings.why: A ~75-word editorial changelog sits above the TL;DR, so the first thing a reader and a snippet extractor encounter is housekeeping about the article rather than the answer to 'celiac travel korea'. The intent is still met inside 200 words, but the opening spends a third of that budget on non-answer text.
findings.fix: Move the changelog to the end of the article next to the 'First published April 2026' line, or collapse it behind a details toggle, so the TL;DR is the first content block.

findings.quote: 1. **If you're celiac, start here** — the five stricter rules, up front
findings.why: The 'In This Guide' block is plain text, not anchor links. In a piece this long that costs the reader a screen of scroll without giving them any way to jump, and it forfeits the jump-to-section sitelinks a linked table of contents can earn.
findings.fix: Convert each TOC entry into an anchor link pointing at the corresponding H2 id.

findings.quote: My wife has non-celiac gluten sensitivity (not celiac). Celiac travelers: apply stricter standards than we do.
findings.why: The NCGS-vs-celiac caveat is restated in the TL;DR, again in 'If You're Celiac, Start Here', again in the 'About My Wife' section, and again inside the Tier 1 and Tier 2 entries. The disclosure itself is a strength, but repeating it five times makes the guide read as three overlapping passes and dilutes scannability.
findings.fix: Keep the TL;DR line and the dedicated 'About My Wife' section, then reduce the mid-article repeats to a single short inline pointer back to that section.

findings.quote: The non-Orion entries trace to a Korean blogger's roundup
findings.why: The convenience-store list is one of the most-read parts of a page like this, and several brand entries rest on a 2023 third-party blog rather than a manufacturer source. It is correctly flagged as a lead, which is why this is minor, but it is the weakest sourcing on the page next to the MFDS and Orion citations.
findings.fix: Replace the non-Orion brands with each manufacturer's own allergen page, as already done for Orion, or drop those brands from this page and keep them only in the snacks post where the caveats are fuller.

criteria.note: Nearly every claim is sourced or explicitly marked as the authors' own observation, but one Tier 2 menu-wide GF claim is asserted with no stated basis.
criteria.evidence_quote: Most of the menu is gluten-free.

criteria.note: Product names, brands, links, and all dates (April 2026 publication, August 2026 update, summer 2025 call plus 'a year has passed', October 2023 blogger post) are specific and internally consistent.

The piece states how it knows (visits, kitchen conversations, label reading, a dated phone call, cited pages) and names what that cannot establish, including the inability to audit a kitchen and the NCGS-not-celiac standard.

No absolute guarantees; shared grills, fryers, lines, and facility disclaimers are all addressed, and celiac risk is repeatedly framed as stricter than the authors' NCGS baseline rather than equivalent.
Every source carries a date or retrieval date, elapsed time is called out where it matters, and reformulation risk is stated as a standing caution.
Korean terms, the 밀떡/쌀떡 distinction, and the mandatory-allergen scope (wheat only; barley and rye not covered) are all described correctly.
Reader gets the exact characters to scan, the statute link, a manufacturer product page, a shop URL to check status, and scripts to reconfirm with staff.

findings.quote: Most of the menu is gluten-free.
findings.why: Every other Tier 2 entry states its basis (staff-confirmed, personally confirmed, or explicitly unverified); this one asserts menu-wide GF status with no source or observation marker, so a celiac reader has only the author's word for a safety-relevant claim about a shared-kitchen cafe.
findings.fix: Add the provenance in the same style used elsewhere, e.g. 'the owner told us most of the menu is GF (our visits, 2026) — we have not verified item by item, and the kitchen is shared.'

findings.why: Korean convenience-store egg SKUs include soy-braised and seasoned variants alongside plain boiled ones; 'naturally GF' invites a reader to skip the flip-and-scan step the article otherwise insists on.
findings.fix: Qualify to plain boiled eggs only and note that 훈제/간장-marinated egg packs are sold in the same chiller and must be label-checked.
